list.listitem: Drinking water should contain less than 10 mcg/L of arsenic. C
Chronic arsenic poisoning is associated with abnormal skin findings, peripheral neuropathy, and certain cancers (lung, bladder, and skin). C
A 24-hour urine test for quantitative inorganic arsenic (speciated) is the gold standard for the diagnosis of arsenic poisoning. C
Treatment should be initiated prior to confirming arsenic levels in cases where acute arsenic poisoning is suspected. C

background.definition: Arsenic poisoning is an acute or chronic condition due to ingestion of or exposure to inorganic arsenic. It occurs on a spectrum from mild illness to fatal illness and can be difficult to diagnose.

list.listitem: Two deaths due to intentional arsenic poisoning were reported to US poison control centers in 2003.
Two hundred million people are at risk from contaminated drinking water in Asia.
There is an association between early arsenic exposure and renal cell cancer.
Contaminated drinking water.
Intentional poisoning.
Contaminated food (rice, grains, fish, and treated poultry).
Ayurvedic herbal medication.
Occupational (insecticides, growth enhancer for livestock, and smelting)
Chromated copper arsenic (CCA)-treated wood.
Inorganic arsenic is a naturally occurring element that is toxic to humans; organic arsenic is found in shellfish and is nontoxic.
Arsenic is readily absorbed the by GI tract, and it can also be absorbed by nonintact skin and the respiratory tract.
Arsenic accumulates in the liver, kidney, spleen, lung, and GI tract rapidly and is excreted by the kidney.
Arsenic binds to skin and nails within 4 weeks of exposure.
Drinking water should contain less than 10 mcg/L of arsenic. C
The gold standard test for chronic arsenic poisoning is a 24-hour urine collection with speciation (ie, separating out the inorganic arsenic). C
Arsenic levels in urine greater than 50 mcg/L are abnormal. C
A spot urine collection can be done initially to verify the presence of arsenic. A speciated sample is preferred. C
Hair assays for arsenic are not recommended for the diagnosis of acute or chronic poisoning. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History of diabetes, glove and stocking sensation, more sensory than motor symptoms, and autonomic dysfunction
History of alcoholism, paresthesias of feet, and ataxic gait
Elevated liver function test results, ileus, constipation, myocardial depression
Weakness and tingling in legs, with rapid progression to arms and respiratory muscles
Intermittent, abdominal pain, constipation, neuropathy, and personality changes
History of exposure, abdominal pain, vomiting, neuropathy, ataxia, and anemia

list.listitem: Patients with acute poisoning will usually have a history of exposure to arsenic-containing substances. See for typical signs and symptoms. Neuropathy is symmetric. It is sensorimotor, but usually with more sensory and fewer motor symptoms.
Patients with chronic poisoning may have a history of environmental exposure (eg, contaminated water or soil). Often, there is no history of known exposure. See for typical symptoms and signs.
Order spot urine test to detect arsenic in body. Specify inorganic arsenic with urine testing; organic arsenic is frequently found in urine because of seafood ingestion and is nontoxic.
Do not wait for test results to initiate treatment in cases of known acute arsenic poisoning.
A 24-hour urine test for inorganic arsenic is the gold standard for quantifying the amount of arsenic exposure.
Blood arsenic levels can be used in cases of chronic poisoning; the results are equivalent to urine results.
Hair samples not accurate because of contamination and poor reliability at many laboratories. There are no data about accuracy of nail samples.
Spot urine arsenic levels greater than 50 mcg/L are abnormal.
Other recommended tests: CBC, UA, liver and renal function tests, and EKG. Also obtain an abdominal x-ray in cases of acute ingestion.

If acute poisoning is suspected (history of ingesting an arsenic-containing compound with typical symptoms; see ) obtain a spot urine analysis for inorganic arsenic and a 24-hour urine test for quantitative inorganic arsenic.

Suspect chronic poisoning if there is a possible history of environmental arsenic exposure; in chronic poisoning there is often no history of ingestion, but symptoms are present. (see ) Order spot urine analysis for inorganic arsenic and a 24-hour urine test for quantitative inorganic arsenic. Blood testing is not always useful.
See Differential Diagnosis.
For suspected cases of acute arsenic toxicity (based on history of ingestion and treatment), initiate chelation without waiting for results of arsenic testing in blood or urine. C
Chelation should begin with British anti-Lewisite 3 to 5 mg/kg IM every 4 hours; change to 2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid 10 mg/kg divided thrice per day for 5 days, then twice a day. C
Acute toxicity: No studies available on the effectiveness of treatment. All recommendations are consensus opinion.
Treatment should be initiated in patients with a history of arsenic ingestion prior to having urine results.
Provide supportive care, monitor for seizures, arrhythmia, and hypotension; begin dialysis if there is renal failure.
If radiopaque material is seen on abdominal film, perform whole bowel irrigation and nasogastric suction to interrupt enterohepatic circulation.

Start chelation if urine results show an elevated level of arsenic or if you suspect acute ingestion: British anti-Lewisite 3 mg to 5 mg/kg IM every 4 hours; when able to take pills, change to 2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid 10 mg/kg by mouth 3 times per day for 5 days, then twice a day. Chelation continues until urinary arsenic levels are less than 50 mcg/24 hours.
Chronic arsenic toxicity: Avoid further arsenic exposure. Chelators were not effective in one small trial.
Vitamin E and selenium are of no benefit.
Spirulina extract plus zinc increases arsenic excretion in urine, but no improvement in signs or symptoms.
Avoid ongoing exposure to arsenic. Patient may not have any food or drink from outside the hospital.
Patient should use a different water source in case of water contamination.
Chronic arsenic toxicity is associated with abnormal skin findings and peripheral neuropathy. C
Chronic arsenic toxicity is associated with lung, bladder, and skin cancers. C
Acute poisoning may have effects on long-term health, including skin findings and peripheral neuropathy. C

Long-term follow-up of 6223 Japanese persons who survived arsenic poisoning in infancy found higher all-cause mortality than the general population, but a lower incidence of several cancer types. SORT C
Symptoms in children with acute arsenic poisoning include fever, skin changes (pigmentation change, desquamation, rash, edema), diarrhea, eye discharge, cough, vomiting, and abdominal distention.
Signs in infants with acute arsenic poisoning include hepatomegaly, abnormal EKG, leukopenia, anemia, and hematuria.
Long-term prognosis in children: proteinuria, abnormal EKG, hearing loss, abnormal refraction, IQ less than 85.
